steps.text: When an editor publishes an article or a visitor registers, something else often has to happen. The Workflows module lets you describe that follow-up as a diagram, with no code. In this video, we'll build a workflow and watch it run.

chapters.title: Why workflows
chapters.subtitle: Reacting to what happens on a site

steps.text: Sites often need to react to what happens on them: an article is published, a user registers, a form is submitted. Doing it by hand is slow, and writing code for every case is costly.
With the Workflows module, you draw the reaction in the admin. Orchard Core runs the diagram each time the event happens, and you can inspect the runs afterwards.
A workflow is a diagram of activities. An event is an activity that waits for something to happen, such as content being published. Only an event can start a workflow.
A task is an activity that does something, such as showing a notification, sending an email, or publishing content.
Each activity has outcomes, which are the exits it can take, such as Done. You connect an outcome to the next activity, and that connection is called a transition.
When the event happens, Orchard Core starts an instance of the workflow and follows the transitions. An instance can finish at once, or wait for another event and continue later.
Orchard Core turns capabilities on as features, and Workflows is one of them. Let's open Tools, Features, and search for workflows.
Workflows is the feature the others build on. HTTP Workflows Activities, Session Workflows Activities, and Timer Workflows Activities add activities of their own, and each is enabled separately.
Let's enable Workflows. The Contents module provides the content events this video uses, once Workflows is enabled.

chapters.title: Create a workflow
chapters.subtitle: A name is all it needs

steps.text: Workflows is under Design in the admin menu. The page lists your workflows. This site has none, so the list is empty.
Let's select Create Workflow. It asks only for a name, and the name says what the workflow does, such as notifying the editors when an article is published.
Let's open More settings. It holds options, such as whether the workflow is enabled and how many instances run at a time. The defaults suit most workflows, so they stay as they are.
Let's select Create and open the designer. It saves the workflow and opens the designer with an empty canvas.
The toolbar shows the name of the workflow, with a link back to Workflows, and the Publish and Discard draft buttons.
The Activities pane on the left lists everything you can add, grouped by category. Search it by name, or show only Events or Tasks.
The canvas in the middle is where the workflow takes shape. A workflow runs when something happens, so an empty one offers events to start with.
On the right, the workflow panel has three tabs. Variables holds named values, Workflow holds settings such as the name, and Issues lists the problems found.

chapters.title: Build a workflow
chapters.subtitle: An event, a task and a transition

steps.text: Under Start with an event, let's pick the Content Published Event. The first event you add becomes the start activity, and its card shows a Start badge.
Its settings open at the bottom of the canvas. Content Types limits the event to the types you choose. Let's pick Article, so other content does not start the workflow.
Each activity shows its outcomes as ports. Let's point at the Done port, where a plus sign appears, then click it and search for Notify.
Let's select Notify Task. It is added to the right, connected to Done by a transition, and it displays a notification when it runs.
A message is required, so the card and the Issues tab flag a problem. Let's type a message and leave the field, and the problem clears.
The designer saves your changes as a draft while you work, and a draft does not run. Let's select Publish, which makes the draft the version that runs.
Let's trigger it. Under Content, Content Items, Edit opens an article in the editor, which has a Publish button.
Let's select Publish. That makes the Content Published Event happen, so the workflow starts. The Notify Task shows its message, next to the notification Orchard Core adds when content is published.
Back in Design, Workflows, the workflow has an Instances badge, because each run of a workflow is kept as an instance.
The page counts the instances by status, and this one is Finished. Let's open it to see the activities that ran, highlighted on the diagram.

chapters.title: What else workflows can do
chapters.subtitle: More events, more tasks, more control

steps.text: HTTP Workflows Activities receive requests and call web services. Timer Workflows Activities run on a schedule. Other modules add events and tasks of their own.
A workflow can branch with an If Else Task, repeat with loops, and keep values in variables. A separate video covers them in depth.
Permissions guard workflows. Manage workflows is needed to build them, and Execute workflows to run them from the designer. By default, only administrators have Manage workflows.
Workflows let a site react to what happens on it, with activities you connect on a canvas. Thanks for watching.
